title: Data from Information Repositories: Sharepoint
summary: SharePoint is a document and collaboration platform, so this sub-technique is the parent behaviour applied to one product whose content and permission model differ from a wiki. Sites and document libraries usually hold the files an organisation actually works from: policies, network and architecture diagrams, project plans, spreadsheets, contracts, and the occasional test credential. Adversaries tend to use the same client interfaces as employees, including the web application, the desktop sync client and the search interface, which makes collection look like routine file access. Many environments also allow sharing links, so an intruder can move data out by creating an external link instead of downloading anything, and that activity appears under the victim's own account. Detection uses unified audit records and access logs: anonymous or external link creation, unusual download volumes, site collection enumeration, permission changes, and sync activity from a device the account has never used. The useful comparison is against the user's own history rather than one company wide baseline.

beginner.definition: SharePoint is a Microsoft tool where teams store documents in sites and libraries. This sub-technique means an attacker searches those libraries for useful files. It is the same idea as the parent technique, but aimed at SharePoint rather than wikis or chat. The attacker usually reaches it with a normal work account.
beginner.whyItMatters: SharePoint often holds the real working files of a company. One account may open many sites, including sites owned by other departments. A sharing link can send a file outside the company in one click. That makes copying data fast and quiet. Without a clear picture of normal use, this activity looks like ordinary work.
howItWorks: The parent technique covers shared repositories; this one focuses on SharePoint sites and libraries.
The attacker signs in, often through the web page or the desktop sync client.
They search across many sites for file names and content that look valuable.
They download documents in bulk, or open them in the browser without downloading them.
They create a sharing link that lets an outside address read the chosen file.
They may change site permissions so their access survives a password reset.
beginner.example: Picture a company library where staff borrow folders from shelves. Each department has its own shelf, but all staff may walk through the whole room. A visitor with a borrowed staff card fills a bag with folders from several different shelves. On the way out they use the photocopier to send copies to a friend outside the building. The librarian only notices later that several shelves are empty.
takeaways: SharePoint holds working documents, so one account can reach many departments at once.
Sharing links move data outside the company and still appear under the victim account.
Compare activity with the user's own history, because normal use differs widely.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique narrows the parent technique to SharePoint.
Describe how search, bulk download and sharing links are used to collect data.
Identify audit events that show external sharing or an unusual download volume.
Explain why a per user baseline matters more than one company wide rule.
Suggest controls that limit broad site access and anonymous sharing links.
